what_it_does: Running a large AI model like LLaMA2-70B requires an enormous amount of fast memory that consumer-grade graphics cards simply do not have. When the model's weights are moved to the computer's main memory or an SSD to compensate, data must travel over a slow connection (PCIe, the slot your graphics card plugs into), creating a traffic jam that makes inference painfully slow. Hermes solves this by splitting the model's weights into 'hot' neurons (roughly 20% of the parameters that do 80% of the real work) and 'cold' neurons (the remaining 80% that do little work per step). Hot neurons stay on the graphics card for fast number-crunching, while cold neurons live on special memory modules (standard RAM sticks fitted with a small processor on board — what the paper calls near-data processing DIMMs) that can do their own arithmetic locally, avoiding the slow connection entirely. A small predictor running at runtime decides on the fly which neurons count as hot for the current input, and a scheduler keeps all the memory modules busy, so the graphics card and the memory modules work simultaneously rather than one waiting for the other.
